chapter: Road bands: Hampton, Crawford and Mingus
title: Childhood visits to Charleston and the effect of Emmett Till
summary: Segregated water fountains in his mother's hometown, and how Emmett Till changed his mind about the South.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was that your first experience in the south?

No, I had been in the south when I was a kid because I used to go to Charleston, North Carolina, my mother’s hometown, and spend a couple of weeks with family like my grandparents and stuff down there.
How was that? Did that affect you?

Well, you know, like when you come from the north and you’re a teenager, you’re not used to any of this stuff. Colored water fountains, when I see a fountain and I’m thirsty then I’m going to go to the water fountain and drink out of it. “No, you can’t drink out of that! You can’t drink out of that one,” that’s what my friends were telling me from Charleston. I’d go over there and drink out of it and, you know, I guess I was bold and whatnot until the Emmett Till incident happened. That’s what changed my mind about ever going back to the south. The few times I ended up going back after that were much different.
